w9-q1: Incorrect — Google was not the partner in launching OpenStack.
Incorrect — Microsoft was not the partner in launching OpenStack.
Correct — OpenStack was launched in 2010 as a joint project of Rackspace Hosting and NASA.
Incorrect — IBM was not the partner in launching OpenStack.
w9-q2: Incorrect — Nova is the compute service, not the dashboard.
Incorrect — Keystone is the identity service, not the dashboard.
Correct — Horizon is the OpenStack dashboard, providing the GUI and an overview of the other components.
Incorrect — Swift is the object storage service, not the dashboard.
w9-q3: Correct — Nova is the compute service, where you launch your instances.
Incorrect — Glance is the image service, not the compute service.
Incorrect — Cinder provides block storage, not compute.
Incorrect — Neutron provides networking, not compute.
w9-q4: Correct — After configuring local.conf, running stack.sh from the Devstack repository installs OpenStack.
Incorrect — docker-compose orchestrates containers and is not the installer used in the lecture.
Incorrect — kubeadm bootstraps Kubernetes clusters, not OpenStack.
Incorrect — ansible-playbook is a configuration tool and is not the installer used here.
w9-q5: Incorrect — Sensor-cloud virtualizes sensor nodes; it does not physically replace sensor hardware.
Correct — Sensor-cloud introduces virtualization of the sensor node, offered on a pay-per-use basis, beyond merely sending data to the cloud.
Incorrect — Sensor-cloud does not claim to eliminate the sink node.
Incorrect — Sensor-cloud is offered pay-per-use, not free and unlimited.
w9-q6: Incorrect — In sensor-cloud, redeployment and maintenance shift to the SCSP, not in a traditional WSN.
Incorrect — The sensor-cloud end-user takes over usage, not redeployment, and only in the sensor-cloud model.
Correct — In a traditional WSN the WSN-user is responsible for ownership, deployment, redeployment, maintenance and usage.
Incorrect — A third-party auditor has no role in redeploying sensor nodes.
w9-q7: Incorrect — The end-user consumes sensor-cloud services; it does not buy and lend sensors.
Correct — The sensor-owner buys physical sensors deployed at various locations and lends them to the sensor-cloud as a business actor.
Incorrect — The SCSP manages the sensor-cloud service; it is not the actor who buys and lends sensors.
Incorrect — The WSN-user belongs to the traditional WSN model, not the sensor-cloud actors.
w9-q8: Incorrect — Traditional WSNs do not have unlimited scalability at zero cost; they have procurement and overhead issues.
Correct — WSNs are hard to adapt to changed requirements, for example repurposing an agriculture WSN for a smart home.
Incorrect — Procurement difficulty, including finding the right vendor, is a limitation, not excessive vendor availability.
Incorrect — WSNs need maintenance, and its overhead is a listed limitation.
w9-q9: Incorrect — Composition across multiple geographic regions is CoV-II, not CoV-I.
Correct — CoV-I forms a Virtual Sensor from homogeneous sensor nodes within the same geographical boundary.
Incorrect — CoV-I is a composition method, not a pricing model.
Incorrect — CoV-I is a composition method, not a caching mechanism.
w9-q10: Incorrect — The External Cache is the source the Internal Cache may re-cache from, not the one serving end-user requests.
Incorrect — The Sensor Cache is not the cache that handles end-user requests directly.
Incorrect — A Distributed Cache is not the cache named for handling end-user requests here.
Correct — The Internal Cache handles end-user requests and decides whether to serve directly or re-cache from the External Cache.
w9-q11: Incorrect — Caching is useful because conditions often change slowly, not extremely fast.
Incorrect — Caching does not remove the need for a sensor-owner.
Incorrect — Caching does not replace virtualization.
Correct — Environmental conditions often change slowly, so repeated sensing wastes energy; adaptive caching avoids this.
w9-q12: Incorrect — Google did not coin the term fog computing.
Incorrect — Amazon did not coin the term fog computing.
Correct — The term fog computing, or fogging, was coined by CISCO.
Incorrect — IBM did not coin the term fog computing.
w9-q13: Incorrect — Traditional cloud suffers from huge traffic consuming bandwidth, not excess bandwidth availability.
Correct — The cloud model faces volume, latency and bandwidth limitations, which motivate fog computing.
Incorrect — The issue is the cloud's distance from devices, not too much local processing at the device level.
Incorrect — IoT devices are plentiful, billions of them; their absence is not the issue.
w9-q14: Incorrect — Fog sits closer to devices, not above the cloud layer.
Correct — The fog layer sits between the cloud and the IoT devices, processing sensor data before it goes to the cloud.
Incorrect — Fog is a layer with many fog nodes, not only inside each IoT device.
Incorrect — Fog extends the cloud closer to devices and does not replace it.
w9-q15: Incorrect — Transient storage is a required fog node characteristic, so it is not the exception.
Incorrect — Computing facility for quick decisions is a required fog node characteristic.
Incorrect — Network connectivity to devices, other fog nodes and the cloud is required.
Correct — Permanent unlimited archival storage is not a fog node requirement; that is the cloud's role.
